n:
- *This is the vision*: This term introduces the book as a unified whole, covering Isaiah’s prophecies over about fifty-five years, from around 740 to 685 BC. 

- *Isaiah son of Amoz*: Nothing else is known about Isaiah’s family. 

- Jerusalem, the capital city of Judah, was the center of Isaiah’s ministry. Some of his prophecies also relate to the northern kingdom, Israel (called Samaria and Ephraim, {{Isaiah 9:8-21|Isaiah 9:8–21}}; {{Isaiah 28:1-13|28:1–13}}), which Assyria destroyed in 722 BC (see {{2 Kings 17:1-41|2 Kings 17}}).

Isaiah spoke many messages from God to the people and leaders of the southern kingdom.

Messages of judgement are recorded in chapter 1. They are examples of judgement messages that are recorded over and over throughout the book. Isaiah’s judgement messages announced how and why people would be judged. The messages in chapter 1 were about the people and the leaders of the southern kingdom.

Those who were sorry for their sin and repented would be saved from being destroyed. Those who refused to stop sinning would be destroyed. They would be punished for not being faithful to the Mount Sinai covenant.

The people and leaders of the southern kingdom didn’t worship only God. They got rich in ways that weren’t honest. They treated needy people badly. They didn’t do what was right and fair. And they didn’t trust God to save them from enemies that attacked them. Because of this God would allow the covenant curses to come on them.

In chapter 1 God described his people (God’s people) in many ways. He called them Sodom and Gomorrah, children who refused to obey and a prostitute. These were ways to describe how God’s people weren’t being faithful to him. They weren’t living as a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.

God longed to forgive his people and to bless them. But they had to be willing to change and to obey him.
*heavens … earth*: All of creation is called to witness the trial that God has convened against Judah (compare {{Deuteronomy 31:28|Deuteronomy 31:28}}; {{Deuteronomy 32:1|32:1}}).

*The ox knows its owner*: Even an animal recognizes the one who feeds and cares for it. But Judah did not recognize or obey the Lord in this way.

Even so, despite their rebellion, God still spoke to them as “my people.” This shows his continued grace (undeserved kindness) toward them.

The term *Holy One of Israel* often appears in Isaiah as a title for the Lord. God is: 

- the righteous and just King of heaven and earth ({{Isaiah 6:3-5|Isaiah 6:3–5}}),

- the incomparable God, meaning no one is like him ({{Isaiah 40:25|Isaiah 40:25}}), and

- the Redeemer (the one who rescues and saves) of his people ({{Isaiah 43:14|Isaiah 43:14}}).

Because of this, it was a serious and foolish sin for Judah to reject him.

God sent famine, war, disease, and death as punishment. However, God often wanted to change stubborn behavior rather than just punish. 

Because of their ongoing rebellion, the people’s “head” is described as injured and their “heart” as sick. This language shows how serious their condition had become.

The nation suffered physical harm from Assyrian attacks. At the same time, they were spiritually defiled and overcome by sin ({{Isaiah 64:6|Isaiah 64:6}}).
*neither cleansed nor bandaged nor soothed with oil*: Judah's national condition was like an injured person who had not received medical care.

*land … cities*: By 701 BC, the Assyrians had destroyed the infrastructure, captured cities, and devastated the fields (see {{Isaiah 64:10|Isaiah 64:10}}). This fulfilled Isaiah’s prophecy ({{Isaiah 6:11-13|Isaiah 6:11–13}}). 

Those who survived the Assyrian attack learned to heed later warnings of exile to Babylon ({{Isaiah 39:6-7|Isaiah 39:6–7}}). God fulfills his promises, so his warning of judgment on all nations is certain.

*the Daughter of Zion*: Zion, one of the hills on which Jerusalem stands, often served as another name for Jerusalem. 

Zion symbolized God's presence ({{Psalm 46:1-11|Psalm 46}}), his protection of his people, and Jerusalem's strength against enemies. Now, however, the opposite is true. Jerusalem has become weak, like a helpless city under siege and like an abandoned shelter or a shack.

*the LORD of Hosts*: This title refers to the countless angels under the Lord’s command (see {{2 Kings 6:16-17|2 Kings 6:16–17}}; {{Matthew 26:53|Matthew 26:53}}). 

During the exodus, Moses described God as a warrior who fought for his people ({{Exodus 15:1-21|Exodus 15:1–21}}). Ironically, in Isaiah’s time, God fought against Judah because of their wickedness ({{Isaiah 1:24|Isaiah 1:24}}; {{Isaiah 3:1-5|3:1–5}}).

- *Hear the word of the LORD*: Here, *listen* means to obey the law (or *teaching;* Hebrew *torah*) of our God (see {{Isaiah 2:3|Isaiah 2:3}}; {{Isaiah 5:24|5:24}}). 

- *rulers … people*: All levels of society were guilty. 

- Like Sodom and Gomorrah, Jerusalem faced divine judgment for rebelling against God’s laws. Jerusalem might have been completely destroyed like those cities if not for God’s grace ({{Isaiah 1:9|Isaiah 1:9}}; see {{Genesis 19:1-38|Genesis 19}}).

The people had sinned so much that God no longer found joy in their sacrifices. The Lord wanted Judah to stop the religious practices he had commanded them to do rather than to continue them in a manner that was sinful and false ({{Isaiah 1:13|Isaiah 1:13}}). Ceremony cannot replace true godliness.

- The incense with offerings was meant to be a sweet fragrance to the Lord (see {{Exodus 30:7-8|Exodus 30:7–8}}). However, when offered with hypocrisy, it became a disgusting smell and an offense to God. 

- The Lord had designated special fasting days at the temple ({{Leviticus 16:31|Leviticus 16:31}}; {{Leviticus 23:32|23:32}}; {{Numbers 29:7|Numbers 29:7}}), but Judah's sinfulness ruined them (see {{Isaiah 58:1-7|Isaiah 58:1–7}}; {{Matthew 6:16-18|Matthew 6:16–18}}). 

- *solemn assembly*: These holy days were associated with the new moon and other festivals (see {{Leviticus 23:1-44|Leviticus 23}}).

- New Moon celebrations took place on the first day of each lunar month ({{Numbers 28:11-15|Numbers 28:11–15}}). These days included sacrifices, special meals, and rest from work.

- The annual festivals included: 

- Passover,

- the Feast of Unleavened Bread, 

- the Feast of Weeks, and

- the Feast of Tabernacles ({{Numbers 28:16-29:39|Numbers 28:16–29:39}}; {{Deuteronomy 16:1-17|Deuteronomy 16:1–17}}).

*I will hide my eyes from you … I will not listen*: The Lord does not answer prayers from those who live in constant wrongdoing. In this situation, God accused the people of twisting his laws to commit violence against innocent victims.

*Wash and cleanse yourselves*: The people were made unclean by their sin and impure sacrifices. To be clean in God's eyes, they needed to change their behavior, remove their sins, and abandon their evil ways (see also {{Isaiah 1:18|Isaiah 1:18}}).

Seeking justice means following God's standards of fairness and supporting the rights of the oppressed, orphans, and widows—those who are weak and marginalized in society (see also {{Jeremiah 7:5-7|Jeremiah 7:5–7}}; {{Jeremiah 22:3|22:3}}; {{Zechariah 7:10|Zechariah 7:10}}; {{Matthew 23:23|Matthew 23:23}}; {{Matthew 25:31-46|25:31–46}}; {{James 1:27|James 1:27}}).

- God called his people to come and settle their dispute so that he could restore his covenant relationship with them. Judah had to choose between obedience and rebellion ({{Isaiah 1:19-20|Isaiah 1:19–20}}). Isaiah says their sins are "like scarlet" and "red like crimson," the color of blood, which Judah had shed unjustly ({{Isaiah 1:15|Isaiah 1:15}}). 

- *white as snow … like wool*: The people would be radically transformed. God would cleanse, purify, and make them holy (see also {{Psalm 51:7|Psalm 51:7}}; {{Daniel 7:9|Daniel 7:9}}).
Repentance leads to life. Resisting God's will and turning away from him leads to death (see {{Deuteronomy 11:26-28|Deuteronomy 11:26–28}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:1-62|28:1–62}}).
*For the mouth of the LORD has spoken*: This statement shows the seriousness of God's promise. The phrase appears 11 times in Isaiah.
The image of Jerusalem as a prostitute symbolizes Judah's unfaithfulness to God (see {{Jeremiah 3:6-14|Jeremiah 3:6–14}}; {{Ezekiel 16:25-26|Ezekiel 16:25–26}}; {{Hosea 1:1-3:5|Hosea 1–3}}).

*The Lord GOD of Hosts, the Mighty One of Israel,* was usually Israel’s protector ({{Isaiah 31:5|Isaiah 31:5}}). However, in this context, God was coming to take revenge against his own people. Their wickedness had turned them into his enemies and foes.

- *I will turn My hand against you*: God, who was usually Israel’s protector, would now act against them as a judge. However, his purpose was not only to punish. He planned to correct and restore his people.

- *I will thoroughly purge your dross; I will remove all your impurities.*: God would use the exile in Babylon to remove the wicked from among his people and to refine those who would return.

The restoration of the community would include new leaders. These leaders would uphold justice instead of twisting it (see {{Isaiah 1:23|Isaiah 1:23}}). 

Jerusalem would once again be like pure silver (see {{Isaiah 1:22|Isaiah:22}}). The city would again be called *the City of Righteousness* and *the Faithful City*.

Here, Zion refers to the remnant (the small group who remain faithful) within the community. Only those who repent (turn away from sin) would receive God’s salvation and cleansing. They would live in his presence.

Zion was meant to be a strong place of justice and righteousness. God loves what is right. He expected the covenant community (the people bound to him by promises) to reflect his holy standards in the way they lived.

The rebels ({{Isaiah 1:28|Isaiah 1:28}}), who worshipped idols in sacred oak groves and gardens, would become like oaks and gardens suffering from drought. They would miss the life-giving presence of the true God. Those who followed the Canaanite fertility religion of Baal considered gardens and trees sacred, thinking they brought blessings. Instead, they led to spiritual death.

*message* (literally *word*): This heading (see {{Isaiah 1:1|Isaiah 1:1}}) likely introduces the revelation of chapters {{Isaiah 2:1-12:6|2–12}}. The main focus is on Judah, but some passages also include: 

- the nations in general ({{Isaiah 2:2-4|Isaiah 2:2–4}}),

- all humankind ({{Isaiah 2:6-22|Isaiah 2:6–22}}),

- Syria and the northern kingdom of Israel ({{Isaiah 7:1-9:21|Isaiah 7–9}}), and

- the Assyrians ({{Isaiah 10:1-34|Isaiah 10}}).

These chapters have more judgement messages. They also include messages of hope for the future. They are examples of the messages of hope recorded over and over throughout the book. Isaiah’s messages of hope announced ways that God would bring blessing. God would bless the people and leaders of the southern kingdom. And God would use them to bless all nations on earth.

In chapter 2, Isaiah’s vision is about a high mountain in the last days. The last days was a way of talking about a time in the future. The time of blessing would come when Mount Zion was raised up high. Mount Zion was the mountain where the temple was built. Talking about the temple being lifted up was a way of describing something. It described a time when God would be honoured as the one true God. All people groups on earth would recognise that God is the only real God. They would respect him.

That is why in the vision people from every nation go to the mountain. They don’t go to attack Jerusalem or to destroy the temple. In this vision there is no more war ever again. Instead, all nations go to learn how God wants them to live. Then they obey God and live the way he taught them to. This is a picture of all people being made right with God. This is also called being made righteous. People from all nations will live the way God always wanted human beings to live.

That is how God would use the family line of Jacob to bless all nations. Through this message Isaiah invited Jacob’s family line to live according to God’s ways. The message was about a time when God would make his people clean and pure. He would judge those who did evil deeds. And he would wash away their sin. That is a way of describing how God forgave their sin. This would allow God’s people to be in his presence again.

After the Israelites (Israel) left Egypt, God was present with them in pillars of cloud and fire. He promised to be present with them again in those ways. His glory would be like a cover over them to protect them.

- In the Old Testament, the phrase *the last days* generally refers to a future time (see {{Jeremiah 49:39|Jeremiah 49:39}}; {{Ezekiel 38:16|Ezekiel 38:16}}; {{Hosea 3:5|Hosea 3:5}}). In the New Testament, it refers to the period that started with the arrival of Jesus ({{Hebrews 1:2|Hebrews 1:2}}). More specifically, it refers to the time just before the end of the current age ({{2 Peter 3:3|2 Peter 3:3}}). 

- The mountain of the Lord’s house refers to the Temple Mount. This place symbolizes God’s glorious exaltation (see {{Isaiah 6:1|Isaiah 6:1}}) and his kingdom on earth. Isaiah’s focus on God’s supreme kingship comes from his famous vision of God ({{Isaiah 6:1-13|Isaiah 6}}). 

- Isaiah’s prophetic hope was not a narrow nationalistic dream. It included people from all over the world, beyond Judah and Jerusalem.

One day, God's generous salvation will reach beyond Israel and Judah. This will lead nations to come to Zion, not for war, but to receive blessings and live by God's rules. 

Isaiah urged Judah to see the benefits that other nations would gain. He wanted to inspire the people of Judah ({{Isaiah 2:5|Isaiah 2:5}}) to feel motivated and follow the Lord, so they would not miss out on that day. 

This section is almost exactly repeated in {{Micah 4:1-3|Micah 4:1–3}}.

- Human society will change as people follow God's revelation and his ways. 

- Judah had already received God’s teaching and word, but they did not obey it ({{Isaiah 1:10-15|Isaiah 1:10–15}}). However, the nations will be ready to do God's will.

- The kingdom of God becomes clear when conflict and violence stop. It is characterized by peace ({{Romans 14:17|Romans 14:17}}). People will either choose to cooperate or be compelled to stop fighting ({{Psalm 46:9|Psalm 46:9}}). Nations will choose divine judgment instead of war (see {{Isaiah 1:18-20|Isaiah 1:18–20}}). 

- The words *judge* and arbitrate describe God's actions here, but later verses show the Messiah as the one who delivers justice ({{Isaiah 11:3-4|Isaiah 11:3–4}}). When this happens, war will end, and nations will turn their weapons into farming tools. 

- *swords into plowshares*: Compare {{Joel 3:10|Joel 3:10}}, where nations are urged to beat their plowshares into swords.

- *Come … let us walk*: Walking in God's light (his revelation) leads to a glorious role in his kingdom (see {{Isaiah 60:1|Isaiah 60:1}}; {{1 John 1:7|1 John 1:7}}). God is the only light that defeats the darkness of sin and evil ({{Isaiah 9:2|Isaiah 9:2}}). 

People cannot create this light on their own ({{Isaiah 59:9|Isaiah 59:9}}). They must walk in the light God provides, trusting him and obeying his will ({{Isaiah 50:10|Isaiah 50:10}}). 

- The phrase *house of Jacob* refers to Israel's special historic relationship with the Lord and their history of sin and rebellion (see {{Isaiah 14:1|Isaiah 14:1}}; {{Isaiah 48:1|48:1}}).

The prophet warned of judgment and mocked human pride. All human systems (religious, economic, military, and social) will face God's examination and be found lacking on the Day of the Lord. This is the final day in history when God will judge the wicked once and for all ({{1 Corinthians 1:8|1 Corinthians 1:8}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:2|1 Thessalonians 5:2}}; {{2 Thessalonians 2:2|2 Thessalonians 2:2}}; {{2 Peter 3:10|2 Peter 3:10}}; {{Revelation 20:7-15|Revelation 20:7–15}}). 

Sometimes, prophets used the phrase *the day of the Lord* (or others like it, such as *that day*) to describe specific times when God judged wickedness throughout history (see {{Isaiah 13:6|Isaiah 13:6}}, {{Isaiah 13:9|9}}; {{Ezekiel 13:5|Ezekiel 13:5}}; {{Ezekiel 30:3|30:3}}; {{Obadiah 15|Obadiah 1:15}}). On the Day of the Lord, only God will be honored. All human wickedness and pride will be defeated. This glorious day of God's arrival will fill wicked and arrogant people with fear ({{Isaiah 2:10|Isaiah 2:10}}, {{Isaiah 2:19|19}}, {{Isaiah 2:21|21}}).

Isaiah condemned Israel and Judah for their pride and self-importance. He warned them that only God should be honored. All attempts by humans to lift themselves up will actually result in humiliation.

- The Lord had rejected his people to discipline them ({{Isaiah 8:17|Isaiah 8:17}}). Although not permanent, this rejection seriously threatened their hopes for a glorious future. 

- *soothsayers*: These were people who practiced pagan religion and magic. God had clearly forbidden this practice in Israel ({{Deuteronomy 18:10-11|Deuteronomy 18:10–11}}). 

- The Philistines were ancient enemies of Israel ({{Isaiah 9:12|Isaiah 9:12}}; {{Isaiah 11:14|11:14}}; {{Isaiah 14:29|14:29}}, {{Isaiah 14:31|31}}).

Isaiah listed the things people used as substitutes for the true God. These included material wealth and security, such as silver and treasures. They also included military strength, such as warhorses and chariots. People also trusted in idols, which were objects they loved and valued.

This kind of wealth and military power marked the reign of King Uzziah ({{2 Chronicles 26:6-21|2 Chronicles 26:6–21}}). However, Isaiah showed that trusting these things was wrong.

In other places, Isaiah explained how foolish it is to worship something made by human hands (see {{Isaiah 44:9-20|Isaiah 44:9–20}}; {{Isaiah 45:16|45:16}}).

- On the day of God’s judgment, people will try to hide in caves and among the rocks. These were natural hiding places in the rocky land of Judah. Instead of repenting with humility before the almighty God, they will try to escape his judgment.

Kings and leaders, as well as slaves and free people, will all look for protection from this judgment(see also {{Revelation 6:15|Revelation 6:15}}). 

- The *terror of the LORD* rrefers to God’s full and powerful wrath against wickedness. This wrath will be revealed on the day of the Lord’s judgment. At this point, the prophecy moves from speaking mainly about Israel ({{Isaiah 2:5-6|Isaiah 2:5–6}}) to speaking about all humankind. 

The Lord opposes anything and anyone to speaking about all humankind ({{Isaiah 2:11-12|Isaiah 2:11–12}}, {{Isaiah 2:22|22}}).

- A key theme in Isaiah is that the Lord will be exalted and humble people will be restored ({{Isaiah 57:15|Isaiah 57:15}}), while proud and powerful people are humbled ({{Isaiah 26:5|26:5}}). 

- The day of judgment and the day of reckoning are also called *the Day of the LORD*. There are seven references to this in {{Isaiah 2:1-4:6|Isaiah 2–4}} ({{Isaiah 2:11|2:11}}, {{Isaiah 2:17|17}}, {{Isaiah 2:20|20}}; {{Isaiah 3:6|3:6}}, {{Isaiah 3:18|18}}; {{Isaiah 4:1|4:1}}, {{Isaiah 4:2|2}}).

- The cedars of Lebanon were valuable trees used to build Solomon’s Temple and palace ({{1 Kings 5:6|1 Kings 5:6}}) and other important buildings ({{Ezra 3:7|Ezra 3:7}}). The cedars symbolized wealth and power ({{2 Chronicles 25:18|2 Chronicles 25:18}}; {{Psalm 92:12|Psalms 92:12}}; {{Psalm 104:16|104:16}}), but these mighty trees were as nothing before the Lord ({{Isaiah 10:34|Isaiah 10:34}}; {{Isaiah 33:9|33:9}}; see the boast of Sennacherib in {{Isaiah 37:24|37:24}}). 

- The oaks of Bashan were also an image of strength and splendor ({{Ezekiel 27:6|Ezekiel 27:6}}). They, too, will disappoint ({{Isaiah 33:9|Isaiah 33:9}}; {{Nahum 1:4|Nahum 1:4}}; {{Zechariah 11:2|Zechariah 11:2}}).
The prophet used several images of human strength to explain {{Isaiah 2:11-12|Isaiah 2:11–12}}.

*every stately vessel*: This refers to large, decorated sea-going ships. These ships were a sign of wealth and economic success.

They showed that a nation was strong in trade and rich in resources.
*that day*: This refers to the Day of the LORD (see {{Isaiah 13:4-13|Isaiah 13:4–13}}).

Animals such as rodents and bats live in dark, underground places. They avoid the light and stay hidden.

In the same way, those who worship idols will try to hide from the Lord’s judgment. They will seek dark places instead of turning to God in repentance.

- The prophecy of judgment in {{Isaiah 2:6-21|Isaiah 2:6–21}} between two related calls to action. First, the people are urged to trust the Lord ({{Isaiah 2:5|Isaiah 2:5}}). Then they are warned not to trust in human beings ({{Isaiah 2:22|Isaiah 2:22}}). 

- Human strength does not last. It is weak and short-lived, like a person’s breath (see {{Psalm 90:1-17|Psalm 90}}).
*remove … food and water*: Long ago, God warned of famine. It could lead to terrible conditions and desperate acts as a judgment for wickedness ({{Leviticus 26:26-29|Leviticus 26:26–29}}).

These verses continue discussing judgment against Israel's leaders (see {{Isaiah 1:23-25|Isaiah 1:23–25}}). Removing leaders at all levels would let the mob take over. Chaos and famine would turn Judah and Jerusalem into a social wasteland.

On the day of judgment, all military, civil, judicial, and religious leaders will be removed ({{Isaiah 39:7|Isaiah 39:7}}; {{2 Kings 24:14-16|2 Kings 24:14–16}}). God will eventually provide good leaders again ({{Isaiah 1:26|Isaiah 1:26}}), but not those who use pagan methods of revelation ({{Isaiah 47:9|47:9}}, {{Isaiah 47:12-13|12–13}}; see {{Deuteronomy 18:10-12|Deuteronomy 18:10–12}}).

Conditions would be so severe that even boys and toddlers could become candidates for office. Isaiah might have meant that adult leaders would be so reduced in number that only children would be left to take on the role. 

Alternatively, he might have meant that the new leaders would be as immature, unwise, strong-willed, and inexperienced as children.

Things would be so bad (*this heap of rubble*) that no one would want to lead. The people would become so desperate that anyone offering food or clothes could lead them ({{Isaiah 3:7|Isaiah 3:7}}). However, no one would actually have food or clothing (see {{Isaiah 4:1|Isaiah 4:1}}).

- The weakness of human strength and society can be seen as a form of divine judgment. 

- *His glorious presence*: The people of Judah were openly wicked, like the people of Sodom ({{Isaiah 3:9|Isaiah 3:9}}; see also {{Isaiah 1:9-10|1:9–10}}).
*The expression on their faces*: At this time, the people openly defied God.
The godly, that is, the righteous remnant (the faithful people who remain loyal to God), will receive God’s reward (see {{Isaiah 40:10|Isaiah 40:10}}).
Those who do wrong and act unfairly will face God's just punishment.

The Lord is both the prosecutor and the supreme judge in this trial against his people.

A prosecutor is someone who brings charges in court. A judge is the one who decides the case. In this passage, the Lord fills both roles.

- *elders and leaders*: Wicked and abusive leadership by ungodly and incompetent leaders hinders God's purpose for his people (see also {{Isaiah 3:12|Isaiah 3:12}}). Therefore, leaders face stricter judgment because they are responsible for the well-being of those they lead.

- *the vineyard*: See the Song of the Vineyard ({{Isaiah 5:1-7|Isaiah 5:1–7}}).

The Lord cares for the poor. These were the marginalized and oppressed (people pushed aside and treated unfairly; see {{Isaiah 1:17|Isaiah 1:17}}). But God is their protector (see {{Isaiah 25:4|25:4}}). 

God asked his people to share his concern for the poor. But instead of helping the poor, many Israelites exploited them to gain wealth (see {{Isaiah 3:14|Isaiah 3:14}}). They used their power to take advantage of those who could not defend themselves.

- The dramatic descriptions show how the people of Jerusalem loved their refined way of life. They proudly showed their self-reliance, power, and prestige. 

- *daughters of Zion*: See “Zion” Theme Note.

TThis passage applies the prophet’s teaching on arrogance (see {{Isaiah 2:11-12|Isaiah 2:11–12}}) to the people of Jerusalem. An alternate understanding is that this passage applies specifically to the women of Jerusalem.

*take away their finery*: In a reversal of fortune, the affluent (wealthy) and proud people of Jerusalem would suffer disgrace (public shame). Wealthy women often wore expensive and beautiful clothing or jewelry ({{Isaiah 3:18|Isaiah 3:18}}). 

This *finery* probably included amulets (small objects people believed could protect them from evil). The people wore these items to keep harm away. But these objects could not prevent the disaster of judgment. 

These beautiful items were also status symbols. They showed wealth, importance, and financial security. The people trusted in these outward signs of success.
*Your men will fall … in battle*: Part of the city’s hopeless destitution (extreme poverty and loss) would be the deaths of the men.

During Isaiah’s ministry, Jerusalem’s population was greatly reduced. War, famine (lack of food), and disease caused many deaths ({{Isaiah 3:1-3|Isaiah 3:1–3}}; {{Isaiah 6:13|6:13}}; {{Isaiah 14:30|14:30}}; {{Isaiah 22:2|22:2}}; {{Isaiah 37:4|37:4}}). 

So many men died that few were left in the city. This created a serious absence of leadership (see {{Isaiah 3:1-12|Isaiah 3:1–12}}). Without strong leaders, the city became weak and unstable.

Even worse conditions were coming. In 734–732 BC, Judah faced war with an alliance(a military agreement) between Syria and Israel ({{2 Chronicles 28:1-27|2 Chronicles 28}}). Later, from 605 to 586 BC, Babylon conquered Judah. Jerusalem was destroyed and fell to its enemies.

- The *Branch* likely refers to the remnant (the faithful people who remain) who would form Israel’s new beginning after the exile (see {{Isaiah 6:13|Isaiah 6:13}}). Some understand the branch as the ideal descendant of David, the Messiah (God’s chosen king; see {{Isaiah 11:1|Isaiah 11:1}}; {{Jeremiah 23:5|Jeremiah 23:5}}; {{Jeremiah 33:15-16|33:15–16}}; {{Zechariah 3:8|Zechariah 3:8}}; {{Zechariah 6:12|6:12}}). 

- Isaiah describes a beautiful and glorious change. The people had experienced shame and disgrace ({{Isaiah 3:17-25|Isaiah 3:17–25}}). Now they would experience fertility (fruitfulness) and beauty. This change would show God’s presence and blessing among the remnant ({{Isaiah 4:6|4:6}}). 

- Even the land would change. The fruit of the land and nature itself would move from desolation (emptiness and ruin) to glory. Isaiah compares this future to the garden of Eden (see {{Isaiah 51:3|Isaiah 51:3}}; {{Isaiah 65:22|65:22}}). The message of renewal finds its ultimate fulfillment in the new creation (see {{Romans 8:19-27|Romans 8:19–27}}; {{2 Corinthians 5:17|2 Corinthians 5:17}}; {{Galatians 6:15|Galatians 6:15}}; {{Ephesians 2:15|Ephesians 2:15}}; {{Ephesians 4:24|4:24}}; {{Revelation 21:22-27|Revelation 21:22–27}}). 

- Those who survive in Israel (the remnant) would be the true citizens of Zion. They would belong to the renewed people of God and share in his promised restoration.

In bold contrast to the desperate picture in {{Isaiah 3:16-4:1|Isaiah 3:16–4:1}}, this prophecy brings salvation and hope. Instead of shame and loss, it promises cleansing, consecration (being set apart for holy use), and renewal. God would cleanse his people from their sin. He would make the remnant holy. He would restore his presence among them.

The imagery in {{Isaiah 4:5-6|Isaiah 4:5–6}} alludes to Israel’s exodus from Egypt. At that time, the Lord guided and protected the people with a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night. Isaiah uses this picture to describe Israel’s future restoration. Just as God once led his people out of Egypt, he would lead them out of exile. Their return would be like a second exodus.

- To be holy was the requirement for citizenship in Zion. Zion is the place where God dwells in his glorious majesty (see {{Isaiah 6:3|Isaiah 6:3}}; {{Hebrews 12:14|Hebrews 12:14}}). 

- The remnant would have their names recorded among the living in the Book of Life ({{Exodus 32:32|Exodus 32:32}}; {{Daniel 12:1|Daniel 12:1}}; {{Malachi 3:16|Malachi 3:16}}; {{Revelation 3:5|Revelation 3:5}}; {{Revelation 20:12|20:12}}).
God’s judgment has a purifying effect on his covenant people (see {{Malachi 3:3|Malachi 3:3}}). Justice must be satisfied before restoration can be offered.

The references to a canopy of cloud and smoke and flaming fire recall God’s continuous presence and protection during the exodus from Egypt ({{Exodus 13:21-22|Exodus 13:21–22}}; {{Exodus 14:21-22|14:21–22}}).

*shelter* (literally *shadow*): See {{Isaiah 32:2|Isaiah 32:2}}; God's protection would keep the remaining people safe from enemies and the destruction he would bring upon the wicked ({{Isaiah 33:14-16|Isaiah 33:14–16}}).

- *my beloved*: This refers to the Lord. The prophet was singing this song on the Lord’s behalf.

- At first, the song seems like a love song. But by {{Isaiah 5:3|Isaiah 5:3}}, readers realize it is actually a complaint. 

- For more on Israel as God’s vineyard, see also {{Isaiah 3:14|Isaiah 3:14}}; {{Matthew 21:33-46|Matthew 21:33–46}}; {{John 15:1-17|John 15:1–17}}.

The Song of the Vineyard is a poem where God criticizes the bad leaders who have hurt Israel, his vineyard. Like some wisdom literature, it first describes a confusing situation ({{Isaiah 5:1-2|Isaiah 5:1–2}}) and then explains its spiritual meaning ({{Isaiah 5:3-7|5:3–7}}). The theme of the vineyard's change appears again in {{Isaiah 27:1-13|Isaiah 27}} and in Jesus's teachings ({{Matthew 21:33|Matthew 21:33}}; {{Mark 12:1|Mark 12:1}}).

The prophet delivered judgment through a song ({{Isaiah 5:1-7|Isaiah 5:1–7}}) and prophecies of sorrow ({{Isaiah 5:8-30|5:8–30}}). Although Israel's future will be pure and in fellowship with God ({{Isaiah 4:2-6|Isaiah 4:2–6}}), it must address the current sinful state of the people and their leaders.

The Lord cared for his vineyard like an expert farmer. He watched it closely, planting the best vines for sweet grapes. God expected much from Israel as his people (see {{Exodus 19:5-6|Exodus 19:5–6}}), so their bitter grapes (their unrighteous deeds) were useless and disappointing (compare {{Galatians 5:22-23|Galatians 5:22–23}}).

- Clearly, the Lord had kindly done everything possible for the vineyard. He was not responsible for the bitter grapes. 

- *I extort you to judge*: Isaiah wanted the audience to condemn the vineyard before revealing that they were the vineyard themselves ({{Isaiah 5:7|Isaiah 5:7}}). This rhetorical tactic is similar to the one Nathan used to confront David ({{2 Samuel 12:1-5|2 Samuel 12:1–5}}).

The Lord promised to turn his vineyard, Israel, into a desolate place because it was only fit for destruction. Later, Isaiah prophesied that Israel would transform from desolation to fruitful vitality (see {{Isaiah 55:13|Isaiah 55:13}}).

Sometimes, the lack of rain was seen as a divine judgment ({{Deuteronomy 28:23-24|Deuteronomy 28:23–24}}; {{Haggai 1:11|Haggai 1:11}}; {{Haggai 2:16|2:16}}). This was particularly harmful to a society that relied heavily on farming.

- The identification of Israel as the vineyard is a surprise. It resolves the riddle of the passage.

- Here, a clever play on Hebrew words is used to accuse Israel. The Lord expected justice (Hebrew *mishpat*) but saw only oppression (*mispakh*) of the needy. Instead of righteousness (*tsedaqah*), there were cries of violence (*tse‘aqah*) against the poor (see {{Isaiah 1:21-23|Isaiah 1:21–23}}). These similar-sounding words make the message memorable.

*Woe*: The first warning of judgment was against oppressive greed. People took properties, like houses and fields, illegally. The new owners were bullies who used every method to get richer at the expense of the poor (see {{1 Kings 21:1-29|1 Kings 21:1–29}}; {{Amos 2:6-7|Amos 2:6–7}}).

This section contains six pronouncements of sorrow. They are six warnings of dreadful judgment ({{Isaiah 5:8|Isaiah 5:8}}, {{Isaiah 5:11|11}}, {{Isaiah 5:18|18}}, {{Isaiah 5:20|20}}, {{Isaiah 5:21|21}}, {{Isaiah 5:22|22}}). These sorrows highlight some of the "sour grapes" produced by the vineyard of Israel ({{Isaiah 5:1-7|5:1–7}}).
As with drought ({{Isaiah 5:5-6|Isaiah 5:5–6}}), the reduction of crops was at times a divine judgment (see {{Haggai 1:6|Haggai 1:6}}, {{Haggai 1:9|9}}; {{Haggai 2:16|2:16}}).

*Woe*: The second threat of judgment concerns indulgent lifestyles (lives centered on pleasure and excess). The language in this section shows a life of moral corruption. The people live for pleasure while ignoring justice and righteousness.

These people are self-indulgent and content. They do not think about the Lord. They are too busy enjoying their drunken parties to consider why things went wrong. They do not reflect on why God sent no rain or why they lost a battle.

- Israel and Judah would go into exile to Assyria in 722 BC and to Babylon in 586 BC. 

- The people did not respond to the Lord because they did not truly know him (see {{Isaiah 1:3|Isaiah 1:3}}). They likely knew about him, but their behavior showed that they did not have a close relationship with him.
The grave (Hebrew *Sheol*) represented the place of the dead in ancient Near Eastern thinking (see {{Isaiah 14:9|Isaiah 14:9}}).
God's rule is always fair and right, and he will be honored for his justice. When he is honored, oppressors will face judgment (see {{Isaiah 1:21-23|Isaiah 1:21–23}}).
God's ropes were "cords of kindness, with ropes of love" for Israel ({{Hosea 11:4|Hosea 11:4}}).
*Woe*: The third threat of judgment was against those who mocked and openly disrespected God's authority.

- The people challenged God to hurry and act. They wanted him to prove that he truly exists and rules the world.

The verb *hurry* translates two Hebrew verbs: 

- *maher* (“be quick”)

- *khush* (“be speedy”)

These same words appear in the name *Maher-shalal-hash-baz* ({{Isaiah 8:1|Isaiah 8:1}}). 

- God had revealed his plan to Isaiah. The people did not understand that God’s purposes would turn against them. Instead of bringing the kind of help they expected, God’s action would bring judgment.

- *Woe*: The fourth threat of judgment was against a lack of integrity. 

- *evil good … darkness to light … sweet with bitter*: This distorted view of life corrupts God's holy order.

*Woe*: The fifth threat of judgment was about the folly (foolishness) of self-deception. Self-deception means lying to oneself. The people believed they were wise and clever. They trusted their own understanding instead of trusting the Lord.
*Woe*: The sixth threat of judgment was against the indulgent lifestyle of the wicked.

- The image of rotting roots reflects human transience (the short and fragile nature of human life; see {{Isaiah 11:1|Isaiah 11:1}}; {{Isaiah 27:6|27:6}}; {{Isaiah 37:31|37:31}}). 

- To despise the Lord’s word means to reject or ignore it. It means living without concern for obeying what God has said.

This attitude leads to folly (foolish living) and ruin ({{Proverbs 1:30|Proverbs 1:30}}; {{Proverbs 5:12|5:12}}; {{Proverbs 15:5|15:5}}).

*mountains quake*: This describes God’s wrath against sinners. The prophets often express God’s anger as the shaking of the earth’s foundations ({{Isaiah 13:13|Isaiah 13:13}}; {{Isaiah 23:11|23:11}}; {{Isaiah 24:18-19|24:18–19}}; {{Isaiah 29:6|29:6}}; {{Isaiah 54:10|54:10}}). God’s appearance in judgment or salvation through natural events is called a *theophany* (a visible display of God's presence). In these moments, God reveals himself through smoke, darkness, lightning, or earthquake (see {{Isaiah 6:1-4|Isaiah 6:1–4}}, {{Isaiah 6:6|6}}; {{Isaiah 13:13|13:13}}; {{Exodus 19:18-19|Exodus 19:18–19}}; {{Psalm 18:7-15|Psalm 18:7–15}}; {{Micah 1:3-4|Micah 1:3–4}}; {{Revelation 8:5|Revelation 8:5}}; {{Revelation 16:17-18|16:17–18}}; {{Revelation 18:21-22|18:21–22}}).

- The signal was a *banner* raised on a long pole. It was often placed on a high hill so people could see it from far away (see also {{Isaiah 13:2|Isaiah 13:2}}; {{Isaiah 18:3|18:3}}; {{Isaiah 30:17|30:17}}). 

In Isaiah, the phrase *a banner for the distant nations* appears many times. Sometimes it calls nations to join in battle, as in this passage. In other places, it calls them to share in salvation ({{Isaiah 11:10|Isaiah 11:10}}, {{Isaiah 11:12|12}}; {{Isaiah 49:22|49:22}}; {{Isaiah 62:10|62:10}}). 

- The *distant nations *here refer to the Assyrians and Babylonians. God used them as instruments (tools) of judgment. Assyria conquered Israel in 722 BC. Babylon destroyed Judah and Jerusalem in 586 BC. 

Isaiah describes them as wild animals called in to trample the vineyard ({{Isaiah 5:5|Isaiah}}{{Isaiah 5:1-7|5:1–7}}). They would fiercely attack Israel and Judah until God's judgment was complete ({{Isaiah 5:27-30|Isaiah 5:27–30}}).

- *that day*: see study note on Isaiah 2:5–22. 

- In Old Testament prophecy, darkness often represents God’s alienation (separation), wrath, and judgment (see also {{Isaiah 8:22|Isaiah 8:22}}). By contrast, light stands for God’s holy presence and blessing (see especially {{Isaiah 60:2|Isaiah 60:2}}, {{Isaiah 60:19|19}}).

- When King Uzziah died, the Assyrians began to regain control in the ancient Near East. This started a period dominated by major world powers: 

- Assyria,

- Babylonia,

- Persia,

- Greece, and

- Rome.

- *I saw the Lord*: The term *Lord* (Hebrew *’adonay*) can refer to human rulers or to God. God is the ultimate King over all nations and rulers.

- *on a throne*: The apostle John also had a vision of God's heavenly throne (see {{Revelation 4:2|Revelation 4:2}}; {{Revelation 7:10|7:10}}; {{Revelation 21:5|21:5}}). 

- Isaiah says that the train (the flowing edge) of the Lord’s robe filled the temple. If only the train of his robe filled the temple, this suggests how great and majestic the Lord himself must be. The robe is only a small part of what Isaiah sees. Yet even that part fills the sacred space.

Isaiah’s great vision of the Lord as King on his throne was a turning point in his life. This vision shaped his work as a prophet.

Scholars understand the historical setting of this event in two main ways:

- Some see {{Isaiah 6:1-13|Isaiah 6}} as Isaiah's original call to ministry. This would mean {{Isaiah 1:1-5:30|Isaiah 1–5}} and {{Isaiah 7:1-12:6|7–12}} belong to the time of King Ahaz. Ahaz began to rule after King Uzziah died({{Isaiah 6:1|Isaiah 6:1}}). 

If this is correct, Isaiah’s call did not appear at the beginning of the book for literary reasons. Perhaps the author placed the call in {{Isaiah 6:1-13|chapter 6}} to end {{Isaiah 1:1-5:30|chapters 1–5}} and introduce {{Isaiah 7:1-12:6|chapters 7–12}}. 

Isaiah’s personal cleansing and commissioning show what the whole nation needed. The people also needed to turn back to God if they were to fulfill their calling to be God’s light to the world.

- Others believe that {{Isaiah 1:1-12:6|chapters 1–12}} follow a chronological order (in the order events happened).

In this view, chapter 6 does not describe Isaiah’s first call. Instead, it describes a recommissioning. This means God sent Isaiah again to serve in a new way.

This new stage of ministry took place during the time of Ahaz. During this period, people would reject Isaiah’s message.

Supporters of this interpretation refer to {{Isaiah 2:7-9|Isaiah 2:7–9}}; {{Isaiah 3:16-24|3:16–24}}; and {{Isaiah 5:8-14|5:8–14}}. They argue that these sections describe a time of wealth, military strength, pride, and luxury. These conditions fit the reign of Uzziah but not the reign of Ahaz.

Isaiah had been set apart by God. This is clear through the story told in chapter 6. Isaiah was in the temple but was able to see more than what was around him. He was allowed to see things in the heavenly world. In a vision he saw God ruling as King. Isaiah recognised how holy God is. This made him recognise how he and his people were full of sin.

God sent Isaiah to speak messages to the people and leaders of Israel. Isaiah shared these messages over and over again in many different ways. He spoke them out loud when talking to King Ahaz. He spoke them to the leaders and people through poems and songs. He wrote them down on large pieces of paper for everyone to see. He also wrote them on scrolls he closed with seals and gave to his followers. Some messages he shared through an action of prophecy. One example of this was having a son and naming him what God commanded.

Isaiah didn’t serve as a prophet by himself. His wife was also a prophet and their children were an important part of his work. The messages that Isaiah spoke were true because they were from God. This became clear when things he announced happened later. One example of this was when Isaiah prophesied to Ahaz about a child named Immanuel. This child was a sign for Ahaz that God would save the southern kingdom. God would save them from the armies of Aram and of the northern kingdom. The story about this is recorded in 2 Kings 16:5–9.

Many years later Matthew understood something about Isaiah’s prophecy about Immanuel. It was also a prophecy about Jesus (Matthew 1:22–23).

The mighty seraphim are heavenly beings not mentioned elsewhere in Scripture (though similar living creatures appear in {{Revelation 4:6-9|Revelation 4:6–9}}; {{Revelation 15:8|15:8}}). The Hebrew term *seraphim* may be related to a word that means “to burn.” This suggests an association with fire. Their name may point to their shining or fiery nature.

In Isaiah’s vision, each seraph had six wings. With two wings they covered their faces. This showed reverence and humility. Even these powerful heavenly beings did not look directly at God’s glory.

- The repeated use of the word *holy* shows that the Lord is completely set apart from all creation.

- *all the earth is full*: The Hebrew text does not include a verb in this line. Because of this, translators understand the seraphim’s words in two possible ways. 

- The earth may already be filled with God’s glory through creation, even though sin has damaged it. 

- The earth may be filled with the Lord’s glory in the future, when he fully establishes his rule as King over the earth. 

Both understandings point to the same truth. One day, the Lord’s glorious presence will be known more fully on earth. This will happen even though humankind is sinful and wicked nations are powerful.

God also revealed His glory in a greater way through the incarnation, when the Son of God became human ({{John 12:41|John 12:41}}; {{2 Corinthians 3:18|2 Corinthians 3:18}}; {{2 Corinthians 4:4-7|4:4–7}}).

*Woe is me, for I am ruined*: The prophet felt unworthy of the vision. He was painfully aware of his personal uncleanness (*unclean lips*) when compared to the holiness of God. Isaiah knew that he was unworthy to speak the pure word of God, as were his people.

*your iniquity is removed and your sin is atoned for*: The prophet's experience of forgiveness anticipated Israel's need for national forgiveness and cleansing ({{Isaiah 43:25|Isaiah 43:25}}; {{Isaiah 44:22|44:22}}; see study note on Isaiah 39:6–7).

- *Who will go for Us?*: The Lord spoke in the presence of his angels. The Bible sometimes describes this gathering as a heavenly council (a group of heavenly beings who stand before God; see also {{1 Kings 22:19-22|1 Kings 22:19–22}}; {{Jeremiah 23:18|Jeremiah 23:18}}, {{Jeremiah 23:22|22}}). 

- *Here am I*: Isaiah answered quickly and willingly. God had just forgiven and cleansed him from sin. Because of this grace (God’s undeserved kindness), Isaiah was ready to serve.

He committed himself to a lifetime of ministry (service for God).

*never understanding … never perceiving*: The prophet's words revealed the true feelings of his audience. The people were so deep in sin that hearing the truth pushed them further from God instead of closer (for example, Ahaz, {{Isaiah 7:1-25|Isaiah 7}}). Yet, the truth needed to be spoken. 

Jesus also used this principle in his own preaching ({{Matthew 13:14-15|Matthew 13:14–15}}; {{Luke 8:10|Luke 8:10}}; {{Luke 19:42|19:42}}; {{John 12:40|John 12:40}}; see also {{Acts 28:26-27|Acts 28:26–27}}; {{Romans 11:8|Romans 11:8}}).

- Isaiah was God’s messenger. Through his message, the wicked became more blind and deaf (they refused to see and hear the truth). But those who honored God gained spiritual sight and hearing (they understood and obeyed; see also {{Isaiah 29:9-10|Isaiah 29:9–10}}, {{Isaiah 29:18|18}}; {{Isaiah 35:5|35:5}}; {{Isaiah 42:7|42:7}}, {{Isaiah 42:16-19|16–19}}; {{Isaiah 43:8|43:8}}; {{Isaiah 56:10|56:10}}; {{Isaiah 59:10|59:10}}). 

- *turn and be healed*: The Lord was ready to heal those who truly repented, but not those who only wanted to avoid judgment while continuing their sinful ways.
*How long … until … the land is desolate and ravaged*: During the prophet's ministry (740 to 685 BC), wars, famines, and devastation plagued the nation.

- Even if *a tenth*, a remnant, survives, the judgment would continue until almost all are destroyed. Isaiah often spoke about near destruction or decimation (almost complete destruction; {{Isaiah 9:18-21|Isaiah 9:18–21}}; {{Isaiah 10:20|10:20}}; {{Isaiah 22:4|22:4}}; {{Isaiah 48:19|48:19}}; {{Isaiah 51:18|51:18}}). But Isaiah also kept hope alive. A remnant would survive and begin again ({{Isaiah 7:21-22|7:21–22}}; {{Isaiah 29:23|29:23}}; {{Isaiah 37:31|37:31}}; {{Isaiah 44:26|44:26}}; {{Isaiah 49:19|49:19}}; {{Isaiah 54:1|54:1}}). 

- *the holy seed will be a stump in the land*: The stump is like the base of a tree that remains after it is cut down. It represents a remnant of holy people (see {{Isaiah 4:2-3|Isaiah 4:2–3}}). From this small beginning, a new leader would come who pleased the Lord ({{Isaiah 11:1|11:1}}).

- Rezin was king of Syria. Damascus was Syria’s capital city.

- Pekah was the king of Israel from 740 to 732 BC. He was a famous warrior ({{2 Chronicles 28:5-8|2 Chronicles 28:5–8}}). 

- Pekah and Rezin began to attack Jerusalem while Jotham was king, from 750 to 732 BC. They increased their attacks during the early years of young King Ahaz ({{2 Kings 15:37|2 Kings 15:37}}; {{2 Kings 16:5|16:5}}).

At one point in his reign, Ahaz faced a serious crisis. The kings of Syria and Israel attacked Judah. They planned to remove Ahaz and force Judah to join them in resisting Assyria.

Instead of trusting the Lord, Ahaz asked Assyria for help ({{2 Kings 16:7-10|2 Kings 16:7–10}}). By doing this, he rejected Isaiah’s call to trust in God ({{Isaiah 7:12|Isaiah 7:12}}). 

The Assyrians defeated Syria and Israel. In time, both nations fell. However, Assyria later turned against Judah and sought to control it completely.

These prophecies occurred when Assyria rose to power. Syria and Israel formed an alliance against Judah ({{Isaiah 7:1-2|Isaiah 7:1–2}}; see {{2 Kings 16:5|2 Kings 16:5}}). God used Assyria as a tool to punish Syria, Israel, and Judah ({{Isaiah 7:1-10:34|Isaiah 7–10}}).
In this long section of the book, the nation of Israel was confronted with a vision of God, similar to how Isaiah was confronted in {{Isaiah 6:1-13|chapter 6}}.

*hearts … trembled*: This means they were very afraid. In contrast, Ahaz’s son, King Hezekiah, faced the Assyrians about 30 years later with strong faith. In 701 BC, he trusted the Lord when Assyria threatened Judah (see {{Isaiah 37:6-7|Isaiah 37:6–7}}, {{Isaiah 37:14-20|14–20}}).
The aqueduct was a place where political negotiations took place later during Hezekiah’s reign (see {{Isaiah 36:2|Isaiah 36:2}}).

- *Do not be afraid*: This was a “do not fear” prophecy, which appears often in Isaiah. In these messages, the Lord assures his people that he is with them and will carry out his plan.

- *two smoldering stubs of firewood*: This image shows that Rezin and Pekah were weak threats. If Ahaz had trusted God’s view, he would have seen that they were about to disappear.
The son of Tabeel, otherwise unknown, was obviously sympathetic to Israel’s and Syria’s resistance against Assyria.

- The Assyrian kings Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal had Israel resettled with people from other places within 65years (by 670 BC; see {{2 Kings 17:24-34|2 Kings 17:24–34}}). 

- Damascus was defeated and destroyed by 732 BC. Samaria was also defeated by 722 BC.

The last sentence is a play on two Hebrew words: If you do not stand firm (*te’amenu*) in your faith (*ta’aminu*), you will not stand at all. Firm trust in the Lord is essential, especially for a leader of God's people (see also {{2 Chronicles 20:20|2 Chronicles 20:20}}). Leaders must act on their faith to show it exists. 

Ahaz and the people of his time trusted Assyria, their enemy, instead of trusting God. They looked for help from a foreign power rather than from the Lord.

Later, King Hezekiah faced a similar threat. In that situation, he showed faith in the Lord (see {{Isaiah 36:1-38:22|Isaiah 36–38}}).

God would give Ahaz a sign to confirm his promise. This sign would take place before Ahaz’s eyes. It would show that God’s word was true.

Later, Ahaz’s son Hezekiah also received a sign from the Lord (see {{Isaiah 37:30|Isaiah 37:30}}).

*I will not test the LORD*: Ahaz’s answer sounded respectful and faithful (based on {{Deuteronomy 6:16|Deuteronomy 6:16.}}However, Ahaz was likely already speaking with the Assyrians. He had probably already decided to trust them for help in this war. His response sounded spiritual and proper, but his actions showed that he did not plan to trust the Lord.

- This prophecy was fully realized with the birth of Jesus Christ ({{Matthew 1:18-24|Matthew 1:18–24}}). It is likely that it also partially came true in Isaiah's time, possibly with the birth of the godly King Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, or one of Isaiah's children. The similar verb sequence in {{Isaiah 7:14|Isaiah 7:14}} and {{Isaiah 8:3|8:3}} (*be with child* … *give birth* … *call*) and the connection between Immanuel and Maher-shalal-hash-baz in {{Isaiah 8:5-10|8:5–10}} suggest they were the same person. 

- The name *Immanuel* means "God with us." This name symbolized God's presence and protection. God was with Judah:

- during the attack by the alliance of Syria and Israel in 734 BC,

- during the Assyrian crisis in 701 BC, and

- throughout their existence until their fall in 586 BC.

The kingdom of Israel fell during Isaiah’s lifetime, in 722 BC.

Even after that disaster, the promise “I am with you” remained important. God spoke these words to his people during the exile and after they returned home ({{Isaiah 41:10|Isaiah 41:10}}; {{Isaiah 43:2|43:2}}, {{Isaiah 43:5|5}}). 

The fullest meaning of this promise appears in Jesus Christ, the incarnate Son of God. *Incarnate* means that God took on human flesh. Jesus is called *Immanuel* ({{Matthew 1:23|Matthew 1:23}}; see also {{Revelation 12:5|Revelation 12:5}}).

- *By the time He knows enough*: The crisis with the alliance of Syria and Israel against Judah occurred in 734 BC. By 732 BC, Damascus, the capital of Syria, was destroyed. Israel, the northern kingdom, was also defeated. 

- *to reject evil and choose good*: This was to happen by age 12, when a child was considered an adult. In 722 BC, Israel went into exile. 

- *He will be eating curds and honey*: The land would lose so many people that food would become easy to find. Even rich foods, once rare, would be available to everyone.

- Israel separated from Judah in 931 BC (see {{1 Kings 12:19-20|1 Kings 12:19–20}}). 

- *He will bring the king of Assyria*: Ahaz asked Assyria for help ({{2 Kings 16:8-9|2 Kings 16:8–9}}). However, Assyria later turned against him. Judah became a vassal state, which means it was forced to serve and pay tribute to Assyria.

The phrase *on that day* refers to the future Day of the LORD, when God acts to judge and to save. 

Judah would first experience the judgment Isaiah had announced. This would be a warning of a greater judgment still to come. That greater judgment was the exile in Babylon from 586 to 538 BC.

Desolate valleys, caves, and thorny areas were often places where people hid in times of danger (see {{Isaiah 2:10|Isaiah 2:10}}). People who were afraid would run there for safety.

However, Judah’s enemies would still find them. These hiding places would not protect them from judgment.

*shave your head and the hair of your legs, and to remove your beard as well*: In the ancient Near East, forced shaving was a disgraceful act (see {{2 Samuel 10:4-5|2 Samuel 10:4–5}}). Here, it served as a metaphor for the destruction of the country.
Farmers faced almost complete disaster. Fertile fields and lush vineyards would turn into wild grazing lands filled with useless plants like briers and thorns (see {{Isaiah 5:6|Isaiah 5:6}}).

The name *Maher-shalal-hash-baz* means “Swift to plunder and quick to carry away.” This name applies to both Judah's enemies ({{Isaiah 8:4|Isaiah 8:4}}) and Judah itself ({{Isaiah 8:7-8|8:7–8}}). Judah trusted Assyria instead of God, and now Assyria would turn against them and nearly destroy them. God was with them (*Immanuel;* see {{Isaiah 7:14|Isaiah 7:14}}), but his presence would be harmful if they refused to trust him (see {{Isaiah 8:14|8:14}}).

Like the name *Immanuel* ({{Isaiah 7:14|Isaiah 7:14}}), Maher-shalal-hash-baz is symbolic. This child might have partially fulfilled the Immanuel prophecy (see study note on Isaiah 7:14). The ultimate fulfillment of the Immanuel prophecy happened with the birth of Jesus ({{Matthew 1:22-23|Matthew 1:22–23}}).

- *before the boy knows how to cry*: See also {{Isaiah 7:16|Isaiah 7:16}}. 

- Damascus and Samaria were ruined and destroyed in 732 BC. This event fulfilled this verse along with {{Isaiah 7:8|Isaiah 7:8}}, {{Isaiah 7:19-20|19–20}}.
This prophecy connects the sign of Maher-shalal-hash-baz with the sign of Immanuel ({{Isaiah 8:8|Isaiah 8:8}}, {{Isaiah 8:10|10}}).

- The gently flowing waters of Shiloah provided Jerusalem with water. They symbolize God's loving presence and care (see {{Psalm 46:4|Psalm 46:4}}). 

- Ahaz rejected God's sign and promise of protection. He lacked faith ({{Isaiah 7:9|Isaiah 7:9}}). Now the people followed his example by hoping Assyria would save them from King Rezin and King Pekah (compare {{Isaiah 7:7-9|Isaiah 7:7–9}}, {{Isaiah 7:16|16}}).

The mighty flood from the Euphrates River symbolizes the invading Assyrian army (see {{Jeremiah 47:2|Jeremiah 47:2}}). The river would overflow its channels when the Assyrians advanced into Judah. This was a stark contrast to the gently flowing waters of Shiloah ({{Isaiah 8:6|Isaiah 8:6}}).

- *up to the neck*: Judah barely survived the Assyrian attacks in 701 BC (see {{Isaiah 36:1-37:38|Isaiah 36–37}}). 

- *its spreading streams will cover your entire land*: From north to south, Judah was almost destroyed, except for Jerusalem (see {{Isaiah 1:8-9|Isaiah 1:8–9}}; chapters {{Isaiah 36:1-37:38|36–37}}). 

- *Immanuel*: Despite their lack of trust and the resulting disaster, God remained with his people (see {{Isaiah 7:14|Isaiah 7:14}}).
God's plan to save his stubborn people would eventually succeed. God intended to destroy Assyria, just as he does with any proud nation that rejects him or brags about its own power.

This text reveals Isaiah's main message. The issue was fear of the Lord versus fear of people (see {{Isaiah 7:9|Isaiah 7:9}}; {{Isaiah 8:6|8:6}}). When someone fears people, the Lord becomes a trap and destruction is certain (compare {{Proverbs 29:25|Proverbs 29:25}}; see “Fearing People” Theme Note). For those who fear the Lord, he becomes a sanctuary and their salvation is assured.

People saw Isaiah’s message of staying out of Assyrian affairs as treason and part of a conspiracy. However, Isaiah was not engaging in political games. He was sharing God’s message. 

What scared them was the alliance of Syria and Israel attacking Judah (see {{Isaiah 7:1|Isaiah 7:1}}, {{Isaiah 7:4|4}}).

*you shall regard as holy*: This means to give God first place in life and recognize that nothing is greater than he is. 

*He should be feared*: This means honoring God with deep respect ({{Proverbs 1:7|Proverbs 1:7}}). The people of Judah were not to fear Israel and Syria or the Assyrians ({{Isaiah 7:9|Isaiah 7:9}}; {{Isaiah 10:24|10:24}}).

- H*e will be a sanctuary*: God is a place of refuge. 

- *stone … stumbling … rock … offense*: By trusting Assyria instead of God, the people of Jerusalem would fall into a trap as the Assyrians turned against them. However, for those who trust in the Lord, he is faithful and strong ({{Isaiah 28:16|Isaiah 28:16}}; see {{Psalm 118:22-23|Psalm 118:22–23}}; {{Luke 2:34|Luke 2:34}}; {{Romans 9:32-33|Romans 9:32–33}}; {{1 Peter 2:6-8|1 Peter 2:6–8}}).
*law* (Hebrew *torah*): The Torah described how Israel was to live in covenant with God. However, the people quickly forgot these instructions (see also {{Isaiah 1:10|Isaiah 1:10}}).

The command to preserve Isaiah’s teaching suggests that many people did not accept his message. Some may have wanted to silence him and stop his words from spreading.

However, faithful disciples kept his messages safe. They protected and passed on the prophet’s words to future generations.

- *I will wait for the LORD … I will put my trust in Him*: Isaiah’s message about Syria, Israel, and Assyria came true in later historical events. This fulfillment encouraged the faithful to wait for the end of all unjust power structures (see {{Isaiah 8:9-10|Isaiah 8:9–10}}). 

Waiting for the Lord involves submission, prayer, hope, and faith (see {{Isaiah 25:9|Isaiah 25:9}}; {{Isaiah 26:8|26:8}}; {{Isaiah 33:2|33:2}}). This leads to a calm spirit and renewed inner strength ({{Isaiah 40:31|40:31}}). 

The book of Hebrews connects these words to Jesus Christ ({{Hebrews 2:13|Hebrews 2:13}}). 

- God had turned away. The people of Israel and Judah were separated from the Lord because of their sin.

*Here am I, and the children the LORD has given me as* (see the reference to Jesus Christ in {{Hebrews 2:13|Hebrews 2:13}}): The names of the prophet Isaiah and his children held important meanings as signs and warnings. 

Shear-jashub (*a remnant will return;* {{Isaiah 7:3|Isaiah 7:3}}) symbolized God's faithfulness to Judah. 

Maher-shalal-hash-baz (*swift to plunder and quick to carry away*) indicated the destruction of Damascus and Samaria ({{Isaiah 8:1-4|Isaiah 8:1–4}}) and the desolation of unfaithful Judah ({{Isaiah 8:5-8|8:5–8}}). 

The name of Isaiah (*Yahweh is salvation*) itself signifies that salvation is from the Lord alone. These three names also represent major themes in the book: 

- the remnant (the small group of people who remain faithful), 

- the coming desolation of Judah (the land becoming empty and ruined), and 

- salvation (God’s rescue of his people).

Immanuel (*God is with us*) brings together all of these themes. It also shows that Judah would be protected if the people trusted in the Lord. God’s presence with them was their true safety.

- Isaiah contrasted his message with the advice of ungodly people around him. His message brought light and truth. The message of spiritists led to darkness and death.

- Mediums tried to discover the future through divination (seeking hidden knowledge through rituals). Some claimed to speak with the dead (see {{Isaiah 19:3|Isaiah 19:3}}). However, God had forbidden these practices because they were empty and harmful ({{Isaiah 47:9|Isaiah 47:9}}; {{Deuteronomy 18:9-11|Deuteronomy 18:9–11}}).

The judgement messages in these chapters are against Jacob’s people and against Assyria. Jacob’s people included the northern kingdom. The northern kingdom was also called Israel and Ephraim. Jacob’s people included the southern kingdom as well. The southern kingdom was also called Judah. God was very angry with his people because they were proud.

The prophets, judges and kings didn’t follow God’s instructions for leaders. These instructions were recorded in Deuteronomy 13:1–5 and Deuteronomy 17:8–20. The leaders made laws that were unfair and they took away people’s rights. God used the Assyrian army as his tool to bring judgement against his people. That is how Assyria was the war club that carried out God’s anger. But Assyria’s king didn’t recognise that he had success in battles because God allowed him to. He was proud. He claimed that his own power and strength made him successful. That is why God would bring judgement against Assyria as well.

The messages of hope in these chapters are about a ruler and king who wasn’t proud. In chapter 9, Isaiah prophesied about a child from David’s family line. This child would become a ruler who did what was fair and right. His rule would last for ever. He would be called Wonderful Adviser and Mighty God. He would be called Father Who Lives For Ever and Prince Who Brings Peace.

In chapter 11, Isaiah prophesied again about this ruler. He was called a Branch like the Branch of the Lord in Isaiah 4:2. He would rule with the help of the Spirit of the Lord. That is another name for the Holy Spirit. Life in the kingdom of this ruler would be very different. It wouldn’t be like life in the world that people were used to. Everyone everywhere on earth would know who God is and would serve him. No one and nothing would cause harm to anyone or anything. Isaiah described this by talking about how children would play with animals that are usually dangerous. No harm would come to them. This was a picture of the peace that this ruler would bring.

Jews came to understand these messages of hope as prophecies about the messiah. New Testament writers came to understand them as prophecies about Jesus. Isaiah wrote out songs of praise that God’s people would sing one day. They would sing them after God finished bringing judgement against them. They would sing them once God brought them comfort. Isaiah chapters 40 to 66 talk about this comfort. In the songs in chapter 12 the Israelites recognise that God is their Saviour. They tell everyone about him. They help all nations on earth know God and honour him. These joyful songs celebrate God as the Holy One of Israel.
God gave instructions and teachings through the law and through his prophets, such as Isaiah (see {{Isaiah 8:16|Isaiah 8:16}}).

- Zebulun and Naphtali were northern tribes in Israel ({{Judges 6:35|Judges 6:35}}). The Assyrian invaders, led by Tiglath-pileser III, humbled them in 734 and 732 BC. During the lifetime of Jesus, people connected this prophecy to his coming out from Galilee ({{Matthew 4:14-16|Matthew 4:14–16}}). 

- Galilee of the Gentiles was the area of Israel between the Sea of Galilee and the Mediterranean Sea. The surrounding Gentile nations heavily influenced it culturally, religiously, and politically.

After judgment and destruction, there would still be hope. God promised that the Messiah (God’s chosen one) would come and rule.

In the Messiah’s kingdom, darkness would end and great light would begin. This light would first appear in Galilee. Then it would spread to the whole nation of Israel and finally to the whole world.

The Messiah would defend those who suffer and are treated unfairly. He would bring an end to cruelty and injustice. He would rule with justice (what is right and fair) and righteousness (living in a right way before God). His kingdom would be a kingdom of peace, and it would last forever.

- The people experienced the rule of other nations as a yoke of slavery and a heavy burden. A yoke is a wooden bar placed on animals to control them. Here it describes harsh control and forced labor ({{Jeremiah 30:8|Jeremiah 30:8}}). 

- *the rod of their oppressor*: In {{Isaiah 10:5|Isaiah 10:5}}, the Assyrians are called “the rod of [the Lord’s] anger.” This means God used Assyria to punish his people. But God’s anger would not last forever. When his anger ended, Assyria’s cruel rule over Judah would also end ({{Isaiah 14:5|Isaiah 14:5}}). 

- The Lord had destroyed the army of Midian through Gideon (see {{Judges 6:35|Judges 6:35}}; {{Judges 7:22-25|7:22–25}}).
Burning the boots and uniforms marked the end of the need for instruments of war.

- *unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given*: This child, the Messiah, would be David’s descendant ({{Isaiah 11:1|Isaiah 11:1}}). 

- *He will be called*: These titles describe the kind of king this child would be. They can be understood as four royal names that show the nature of his rule: 

- The *Wonderful Counselor* rules with God’s wisdom ({{Isaiah 11:1|Isaiah 11:1}}; {{Isaiah 25:1|25:1}}; {{Isaiah 28:29|28:29}}; {{Isaiah 40:13|40:13}}). His wisdom is different from the weak and foolish leaders of Judah ({{Isaiah 1:26|1:26}}; {{Isaiah 3:3|3:3}}). 

- The *Mighty God* is an affirmation of the Messiah’s divine nature. It shows that he shares in God’s power and authority. 

- The *Everlasting Father* cares for his people like a father. His care never ends (compare {{Isaiah 22:21|Isaiah 22:21}}; {{Isaiah 63:16|63:16}}). 

- The *Prince of Peace* is a ruler who brings peace, not war.

- Some scholars understand the titles as two longer names instead of four:

- “A Wonderful Counselor [is] the Mighty God”; and

- “the Everlasting Father [is] a Prince of Peace” (on his nature, see {{Isaiah 11:1-9|Isaiah 11:1–9}}). 

- The New Testament identifies Jesus Christ as this promised Son of David ({{Matthew 1:1|Matthew 1:1}}; {{Luke 1:32|Luke 1:32}}; see also {{Isaiah 7:14|Isaiah 7:14}}; {{Isaiah 8:3|8:3}}, {{Isaiah 8:18|18}}). He will establish his kingdom of peace ({{Revelation 19:1-21|Revelation 19}}).

This ruler, like Ahaz, will be a descendant of David. However, unlike Ahaz and the rulers of Jerusalem ({{Isaiah 1:21-23|Isaiah 1:21–23}}), he will trust God and rule with justice and righteousness ({{Isaiah 11:1-3|11:1–3}}). Jesus the Messiah reigns forever ({{Luke 1:32-33|Luke 1:32–33}}).

This prophecy of judgment was against the northern kingdom of Israel. Even though God warned that the Assyrians would defeat them ({{Isaiah 7:1-8:22|Isaiah 7–8}}), the people of Samaria were foolishly confident they could survive the siege.
Israel believed they could replace what they lost with more costly items (see {{Isaiah 2:13-16|Isaiah 2:13–16}}; {{Amos 5:11|Amos 5:11}}).
Rezin's enemies were the Assyrians ({{Isaiah 7:4|Isaiah 7:4}}, {{Isaiah 7:17|17}}; {{Isaiah 8:4|8:4}}). Rezin was the king of Syria (see {{Isaiah 7:1-25|Isaiah 7}}).

God used punishment to call his people to repentance. Repentance means turning away from sin and turning back to God. His goal was not to destroy Israel, but to correct them and bring them back to himself.

However, Israel had become apostate. This means they had turned away from the Lord and rejected him. They refused to repent or to seek the Lord.

Widows and orphans are usually special objects of God’s compassion and care ({{Isaiah 1:17|Isaiah 1:17}}, {{Isaiah 1:23|23}}; {{Isaiah 10:2|10:2}}). However, when they remained unrepentant, they also faced God’s wrath. This means they experienced his judgment. God’s judgment was not based on social position, but on whether people turned back to him.

After the leaders were destroyed, the nation would fall into chaos. With no strong leadership, people would turn against one another.

Civil war would then destroy the nation. It would spread quickly and cause great damage, like a brushfire that no one can control.

Manasseh and Ephraim represent the northern kingdom because they were its largest tribes. These tribes stood for the whole kingdom of Israel.

The two largest tribes of Israel and Judah fought against each other. This likely refers to the war between Judah and the alliance of Syria and Israel. This war is often called the Syro-Ephraimite War ({{Isaiah 7:1-12|Isaiah 7:1–12}}). During this conflict, people from the same family fought against one another. In other words, brothers fought against brothers ({{2 Chronicles 28:1-27|2 Chronicles 28}}). This civil war brought great suffering to God’s people.
*Woe*: This introduces a threat of divine judgment.

This prophecy was spoken against the leaders of Judah. They used their positions of authority for personal gain.

Instead of serving the people, they made themselves rich. They did this at the people’s expense. God spoke this message to confront their injustice and wrongdoing.

- Isaiah asked several questions, but he did not expect an answer. The implied answer was clear. When God punished Judah, there would be no one to help them.

- Disaster first came from the distant land of Assyria. Later, it came from Babylon. These nations became the instruments of God’s judgment.

The Assyrians were God’s instrument in judging Syria, Israel, and Judah. The prophet describes them as a *rod* and a *club*. These are tools used to strike or discipline someone.

God used Assyria to punish these nations. However, Assyria acted with pride and cruelty. Because of their own wickedness, they would not escape judgment.

God announced judgment on Assyria for several reasons: 

- They destroyed other nations without mercy ({{Isaiah 10:7|Isaiah 10:7}}).

- They spoke with pride and dishonored God. They boasted about their own power ({{Isaiah 10:12|Isaiah 10:12}}).

- They oppressed other peoples and took what did not belong to them ({{Isaiah 10:13-14|Isaiah 10:13–14}}).

- They believed they were acting on their own. They did not recognize that God was using them ({{Isaiah 10:15|Isaiah 10:15}}).

{{Isaiah 9:8-10:4|Isaiah 9:8–10:4}} shows that the Lord’s moral law is supreme. This means God’s standards of right and wrong stand above every nation and ruler. The next section explains what this truth means: 

- Assyria was only a tool in God’s hands. Because of this, Assyria was also responsible to God. Like every other nation, it would face judgment for its sin ({{Isaiah 10:5-19|Isaiah 10:5–19}}, {{Isaiah 10:28-34|28–34}}).

- Those among God’s people who trusted in him and obeyed his covenant would be rescued ({{Isaiah 10:20-27|Isaiah 10:20–27}}).

- God would establish his kingdom on earth ({{Isaiah 11:1-16|Isaiah 11}}).

- Judah had a special calling as God’s covenant people. A covenant is a binding agreement between God and his people. However, Judah turned away from the Lord and became a godless nation.

Because of this, they became the object of God’s anger ({{Isaiah 10:4|Isaiah 10:4}}). God’s judgment came not because he broke his covenant, but because they did.

- The word *plunder* translates two Hebrew words, *shalal* and *baz*. Both words mean to take goods by force after victory in battle.

These words recall the name *Maher-shalal-hash-baz *(see {{Isaiah 5:19|Isaiah 5:19}}; {{Isaiah 8:1|8:1}}, {{Isaiah 8:3|3}}, {{Isaiah 8:5-10|5–10}}).

The Assyrians did not understand that they were carrying out God’s purpose. God used them to punish Israel and Judah.

However, the Assyrians acted on their own desires. They killed and looted other nations with cruelty. They did more than God intended.

Because of their pride and violence, God would hold them guilty. They would also face his judgment.

By 717 BC, Assyria controlled the regions north of Judah. These areas had fallen one by one.

Calno was a city in northern Syria. It is called Calneh in {{Amos 6:2|Amos 6:2.}} The Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III captured it in 738 BC.

Carchemish stood on the Euphrates River. King Sargon II captured it in 717 BC.

Hamath was located on the Orontes River. Assyria brought it under control in 738 BC and again in 720 BC.

Arpad was a city south of Calno. Damascus and Samaria were the capital cities of Syria and Israel. Assyria captured Damascus in 732 BC and Samaria in 722 BC ({{Isaiah 7:8|Isaiah 7:8}}; {{Isaiah 8:4|8:4}}).
*whose images surpassed those of Jerusalem and Samaria*: Assyria would make this argument while threatening Jerusalem ({{Isaiah 36:19-20|Isaiah 36:19–20}}; {{Isaiah 37:12|37:12}}).

Assyria destroyed Samaria in 722 BC. This happened during the reigns of Shalmaneser V and Sargon II ({{2 Kings 17:3-6|2 Kings 17:3–6}}). 

Samaria and Judah both worshiped the same God. Because Assyria had already defeated Samaria, the king of Assyria believed he could also defeat Judah.

Any royal power that exalts itself against the Lord is proud and arrogant. The Lord is the Great King over all rulers.

When kings lift themselves up against him, they set themselves in opposition to God. Such pride will not last.

God will humble and crush every ruler who stands against him (see {{Isaiah 2:11-12|Isaiah 2:11–12}}).

*By the strength of my hand … and by my wisdom *(compare {{Isaiah 10:5|Isaiah 10:5}}): Only God is all-powerful and wise. He plans the future and decides which nations will rise to power and which will be defeated.

*axe … saw … rod … staff*: These tools are only as effective as the person using them. Assyria thought it was independent of God's influence. However, their victories were possible only with his permission and to fulfill his purposes ({{Isaiah 10:5|Isaiah 10:5}}).

This prophecy was fulfilled in 701 BC. In that year, 185,000 Assyrian soldiers died.

They were struck down by a plague and by flaming fire. This event marked a sudden and dramatic defeat for Assyria (see {{Isaiah 37:36|Isaiah 37:36}}).

*the survivors*: This refers to a small group who remained alive. This group is called a remnant. A remnant is a small number of people who survive after great destruction.

A remnant from Jerusalem barely survived. However, their safety was secure because God had promised to preserve them (see {{Isaiah 1:8-9|Isaiah 1:8–9}}; {{Isaiah 4:2|4:2}}; {{Isaiah 6:13|6:13}}; {{Isaiah 37:31-32|37:31–32}}). 

These wars taught the remnant an important lesson. They were not to depend on powerful nations such as Assyria for help.

Instead, they were to trust faithfully in the Lord alone (see {{Isaiah 8:13|Isaiah 8:13}}; {{Isaiah 17:7|17:7}}).

In the middle of Assyrian oppression, there was still hope for the remnant. This passage explains more clearly the meaning of the name *Shear-jashub*. The name means “a remnant will return” ({{Isaiah 10:21|Isaiah 10:21}}; see {{Isaiah 7:3|7:3}}; {{Isaiah 8:18|8:18}}).

The promise showed that God would not destroy all his people. Some would return to him and live under his care.

- God had promised Abraham that his descendants would be as numerous as the sand on the seashore ({{Genesis 22:17|Genesis 22:17}}). 

- *Destruction has been decreed, overflowing with righteousness*: God's decision was right and just. It was a response to the people’s continued and stubborn wickedness. God’s judgment did not cancel his promise. He remained faithful, even while he punished sin.
God promised his people that he would be with them and had a plan for them.
Israel’s captivity ended in 539 BC. At that time, many of the people returned from exile. This return is sometimes described as a new exodus because God brought them out of a foreign land again.

*Assyria has entered Aiath*: {{Isaiah 10:29-32|Isaiah 10:29–32}} describes the march of the Assyrian army in poetic language. The cities are listed in order from the north toward Jerusalem.

The army moves closer and closer to the city. When they reach Jerusalem, they are forced to stop and retreat.

God was with Jerusalem. Because of this, Assyria would not succeed. In time, Assyria itself would be destroyed.

This passage may refer to Sennacherib’s invasion in 701 BC (see {{Isaiah 36:1-37:38|Isaiah 36–37}}). However, it could also describe an earlier or later invasion.
